name: Two Pointer
description: Use two indices moving toward or away from each other to solve in O(n).
explanation: The two-pointer technique uses two references that traverse a data structure — often from opposite ends moving inward, or a slow/fast pair. This converts O(n^2) brute-force comparisons into O(n) single-pass solutions. Classic applications: palindrome check, pair sum in sorted array, removing duplicates in-place.

name: Frequency Map
description: Count occurrences using a hash map for O(1) lookups.
explanation: Build a map of element → count, then query it. This pattern appears whenever you need to count, find duplicates, check anagrams, or find the most/least frequent element. Time: O(n) to build, O(1) per lookup.

name: Hash Map Lookup
description: Store seen values for O(1) complement or existence checks.
explanation: Instead of nested loops to find pairs/matches, store previously seen values in a hash map. On each new element, check if its complement/match exists in the map. Converts O(n^2) to O(n). Classic: Two Sum.

name: Accumulator
description: Build up a result by iterating and accumulating values.
explanation: The accumulator pattern maintains a running result (sum, max, string, array) that gets updated on each iteration. It's the foundation of reduce operations. Simple but fundamental — most array/string traversals use some form of accumulation.

name: In-Place Swap
description: Modify an array in-place by swapping elements without extra space.
explanation: Rather than creating a new array, swap elements in the existing one. Uses O(1) extra space. Key technique for reversals, rotations, partitioning, and Dutch National Flag problems.

name: Sliding Window
description: Maintain a window over a sequence, sliding it to find optimal subsets.
explanation: Keep track of a contiguous subset (window) using two pointers. Expand the right side to include new elements, shrink from the left when the window violates a constraint. Converts naive O(n*k) approaches to O(n). Used for: max sum subarray, longest substring without repeats, minimum window substring.

name: Divide and Conquer
description: Split the problem in half, solve each half, combine results.
explanation: Break a problem into smaller subproblems, solve them independently (often recursively), then merge results. Foundation of merge sort, quick sort, binary search. Time complexity often O(n log n).

name: Recursion with Memoization
description: Cache recursive results to avoid redundant computation.
explanation: When a recursive solution has overlapping subproblems (same inputs computed multiple times), store results in a cache. Transforms exponential time to polynomial. Bridge between pure recursion and dynamic programming.

name: String Traversal
description: Iterate through characters to build, transform, or analyze strings.
explanation: Walk through a string character by character, building a result or collecting information. Foundation for most string problems. Often combined with a frequency map or accumulator.

name: Binary Search Variant
description: Apply binary search logic to non-obvious search spaces.
explanation: Beyond searching sorted arrays, binary search applies to any monotonic condition. Find insertion points, search rotated arrays, find peaks, or search on answer spaces. Always O(log n).

name: Basic Recursion
description: Solve a problem by reducing it to a simpler version of itself.
explanation: Every recursive solution needs a base case (when to stop) and a recursive case (how to reduce). Think: what's the simplest version of this problem? How do I get from n to n-1? Foundation for trees, graphs, backtracking, and dynamic programming.

name: Deep Traversal
description: Recursively traverse nested structures (objects, arrays, trees).
explanation: When data is nested to arbitrary depth, recursion naturally handles each level. Check the type of the current element: if it's a leaf, process it; if it's a container, recurse into it. Used for: deep clone, flatten, search, transform.
